rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Earlier prophets’ teachings were transmitted orally, and the present Torah is a written record of tradition whose divine and narrator wording cannot be distinguished; the Qur’an was preserved word for word under God’s scrutiny.
rows.anchor: for the Qur’ ān the Almighty made elaborate arrangements that all of it be composed of His words

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Written preservation of revelation was unprecedented and especially a favor to unlettered Arabs, who thereby preserved guidance intended for all mankind.
rows.anchor: since the Arabs were unlettered they were not fully aware of the use of the pen

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The teaching of what was unknown is primarily the favor given to the unlettered Arab first audience: complete guidance led them from ignorance, and they must honor it.
rows.anchor: the unlettered Arabs were not only bestowed with divine guidance in written form

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sūrah al-Jumu‘ah passage also describes God sending a prophet among the unlettered who recites revelation and teaches the Book and wisdom.
rows.anchor: It is He Who has sent forth among the unlettered a prophet from among

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Quraysh reject guidance arrogantly because wealth makes them feel self-sufficient and indifferent to God; their stated objections disguise this real motive and their love of the world.
rows.anchor: self-sufficient from God and their love for this world

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet is to leave them to their conduct: they will return to their neglected Lord, discover the consequence of arrogance, and find that only God rules and can seize them.
rows.anchor: Finally, they will have to return to their Lord to whom they have become indifferent and fearless

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Those who stop the Prophet or other Muslims from prayer exemplify the earlier rebellion; prayer is a person’s foremost duty to God and deserves respect.
rows.anchor: and other Muslims from praying

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The expression ‘have you seen’ directs attention to something improper or criticizes the perpetrator, like ‘just look at him’ in English.
rows.anchor: are its equivalents in the English language

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The description need not refer to one named person: multiple Quraysh ruffians, not only Abu Jahl, stopped the Prophet and other servants of God from prayer.
rows.anchor: other ruffians besides him too

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The would-be blocker should consider whether the worshipper is rightly guided and calls others to virtue; ignoring that possibility invites God’s wrath and is a satanic act.
rows.anchor: Is not there a chance that this servant of God be on the right path

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The second possibility is that the blocker himself denied and turned away, making himself responsible for opening Hell’s door; the apodosis is suppressed to convey an unspeakable severity, a classical Arabic style.
rows.anchor: Here, a suppression of the overall apodosis has occurred to point to the fact that its severity is beyond words

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The fate of those who deny and turn away is illustrated by 92:15–16, which says the wretched enter Hell.
rows.anchor: Only those wretched creatures shall enter Hell

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The offender should realize that God sees his unrestrained conduct and will justly avenge preventing His servants from worshipping Him.
rows.anchor: the Almighty is watching all his unrestrained behaviour

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The forelock is the forehead and its hair; ‘to drag’ means to seize something in a fist, as 55:41 describes people being grasped by forelocks and legs and thrown into Hell.
rows.anchor: then they shall be grasped by their forelocks and legs

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The second ‘forelock’ is grammatically a بدل of the preceding definite forelock; it can count as definite through its adjective despite lacking the article.
rows.anchor: Though the former is not defined by the article alif

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The harsh wording conveys anger; the forehead represents a person’s honor, and the prostration mark is its greatest honor, so one who refuses prostration and prevents others deserves Hell.
rows.anchor: the greatest honour for a forehead is the mark of prostration that becomes stamped on it

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verses challenge the arrogant to summon their faction while God summons His guards; Badr later demonstrated the Quraysh’s humiliation by God’s guards.
rows.anchor: the Quraysh was humiliated at the hands

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Nādī literally means a gathering or society and here denotes people linked communally, hence a group or party.
rows.anchor: it can be translated as

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Zabāniyah means defenders and can describe police or law enforcers; here it is a temporary divine task force of angels.
rows.anchor: which are temporary in nature

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet is assured to ignore anyone who blocks his prostration and draw nearer to God through it; prayer brings perseverance and divine help, and prostration is its greatest component.
rows.anchor: he should just ignore him and draw nearer the Almighty by prostrating before Him

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Prostration is the objective of the Prophet’s life and his sole means of relationship with God, so he should seek refuge in God through it if challenged.
rows.anchor: The only way to do this is to prostrate before Him

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: To determine a sūrah’s revelation period, tone, addressee, and style are especially useful; the author therefore considers this question after the explanation.
rows.anchor: The most helpful thing in determining the period of revelation of a sūrah is to deliberate on its tone, address and style of address

rows.speaker: some people
rows.claim: One reported view makes the whole of Sūrah al-‘Alaq the Qur’an’s first revelation; the majority instead regards its first five verses as first, based on a report in Bukhārī and Muslim.
rows.anchor: the majority regards its first

rows.speaker: Zamakhsharī
rows.claim: Zamakhsharī records the view that al-Fātiḥah was revealed first and then Sūrah al-Qalam; exegetes both accept and dispute it.
rows.anchor: Zamakhshar ī. He has recorded in

rows.speaker: the proponents of this view
rows.claim: A third view says Sūrah al-Muddaththir was first; its proponents probably mean only its opening verses because the rest has a severity resembling al-‘Alaq.
rows.anchor: The proponents of this view most probably regard its initial verses only as the first revelation

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author considers al-‘Alaq a coherent, single unit: its first five verses share the rest’s severe tone, and nothing in it indicates revelation in two episodes.
rows.anchor: The tone of its first five verses is no different

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Sūrah al-Qadr develops the previous sūrah’s account of revelation as a blessing and written guidance by focusing on the Qur’an’s revelation night and its greatness.
rows.anchor: Now, this sūrah deals with the subject of the revelation of the Qur’ ān itself

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The account tells the audience that the Book is part of a divine plan, revealed under God’s direct supervision rather than human whim.
rows.anchor: this Book is not the result of some human whim or desire

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The revelation is an enduring event tied to a night when important decisions are made and executed; its blessings cannot be gained through another route.
rows.anchor: This event is not temporary or transient in nature

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The revelation night was specially protected from Satan’s interference, keeping the Book free of evil intrusion.
rows.anchor: the night in which it was revealed has been specially protected from his intrusions and interventions

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Although the pronoun in ‘We sent it down’ appears to lack an antecedent, the preceding sūrah supplies it, supporting the Qur’an’s deep coherence between successive sūrahs.
rows.anchor: the placement of this sūrah after the previous one clearly indicates the antecedent

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The emphatic ‘Indeed We’ rejects the claim that the Qur’an came from the Prophet’s desire or Satan; it was revealed by God alone for human guidance.
rows.anchor: it has been solely revealed by the Almighty Himself to provide guidance and direction to mankind

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Laylat al-Qadr is the night when decrees are decided and entrusted to angels for execution, as in 44:3–5.
rows.anchor: the night in which matters are decided and their enforcement entrusted to the angels

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The linked verses show that decrees are entrusted to angels on this glorious night; the Prophet’s commission, warning to Quraysh, and Qur’anic revelation are among them, making these events part of God’s major plan.
rows.anchor: During this night all decrees of wisdom are assigned

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse does not say that the entire Qur’an descended in one night: its first revelation came then after the decision and handover to Gabriel, followed by gradual revelation over twenty-three years.
rows.anchor: All that it necessitates is that after a

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The night’s majesty exceeds imagination because it carries decisions governing the world, like the importance of planning a country’s future magnified to the scale of the universe.
rows.anchor: how can the significance of the Night in which Divine Directives are issued forth to decide the fate of the whole universe be estimated

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Though decrees bring both destruction and blessing, punishment and creation, they benefit humanity overall because they arise from God’s justice, wisdom, and mercy; this explains the night’s description as blessed in 44:3–5.
rows.anchor: all decisions are beneficial to man in their overall capacity and augur well for the future

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The adversaries err by calling the Qur’an soothsaying, poetry, or sorcery: the protected, exalted night allows no evil inspiration to intrude on its revelation.
rows.anchor: revelation are showered by the Creator of the Heavens

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The night is ‘better’ because certain spiritual aims require appointed times, just as crops need the right season and Friday prayer, fasting, and pilgrimage have fixed times.
rows.anchor: there are special days and times of the year which are set aside for special acts of worship

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Prayer on this night may bring nearness to God unattainable across a thousand other nights; ‘a thousand’ can signal abundance or comparative superiority, both pointing to hidden spiritual wealth.
rows.anchor: a lot of spiritual wealth is hidden beneath the veils of this night

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The revelation night fell in Ramadan according to 2:185; because hadith reports conflict on its exact date, the author says it most probably fell in the last ten days.
rows.anchor: The only thing which can be said is that it occurred most probably during the last ten days

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Conflicting reports raise whether the night can fall outside Ramadan and whether it recurs every Ramadan; resolving this requires hadith analysis beyond this tafsīr, which the author invites scholars to undertake.
rows.anchor: which is beyond the scope of this exegesis

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Gabriel and the other angels descend to execute the tasks God assigned that night, as also stated in 44:4–5.
rows.anchor: In this night, Archangel Gabriel and other angels descend upon the earth

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ‘The Spirit’ means Gabriel in context; he is singled out because he holds a very high rank among angels.
rows.anchor: very high rank among the angels

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author parses ‘peace’ as the predicate of an omitted subject; suppressing that subject emphasizes the predicate and makes the phrase hyperbolic, like saying ‘Zayd is justice.’
rows.anchor: supp ressed to emphasize the enunciative

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ‘Peace’ means safety from danger generally and Satanic interference especially; Satan’s forces appear detained until dawn, unable to learn the night’s secrets or disrupt its blessings.
rows.anchor: during this night also these evil creatures are under Divine detention till the rise of dawn

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Bayyinah complements al-Qadr: the Qur’an’s exaltedness is explained, and the People of the Book and Makkan idolaters rejected it from conceit, not genuine doubt, using demands for a sign as a pretext.
rows.anchor: conceit and arrogance which led them to this attitude

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Even if the opponents witnessed the greatest signs and miracles, they would invent excuses to conceal their haughtiness.
rows.anchor: would not convince them in this matter

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Jews initially held back from active opposition because they expected Quraysh to end the new faith.
rows.anchor: they did not take any practical part in opposing this call

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: When Jews began supporting Quraysh, they supplied objections and questions for them to ask the Prophet in order to pester and harass him.
rows.anchor: they were told to ask the Prophet (sws) in order to pester

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: At first the Jews expected Quraysh opposition to end Islam; when it spread, they supplied objections and invented tests, including a heavenly fire consuming a prophet’s sacrifice, to help Quraysh challenge Muhammad.
rows.anchor: any prophethood unless a fire descends from the sky

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The discourse assures the Prophet that Quraysh and the People of the Book will not desist or accept the Qur’an; they would believe only if an angel descended reciting scripture.
rows.anchor: They will only believe when an angel will descend from the skies whilst reading some scripture

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The People of the Book support Quraysh out of enmity despite having witnessed miracles; they remained blind and divided over the religion’s foundational truths.
rows.anchor: In fact, they remained blind even after seeing these

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The conclusion rebukes the conceited who think themselves superior: disbelievers are the worst creatures and face Hell, while unseen faith and righteous deeds mark those with standing before God.
rows.anchor: Only those people are of any status before God who profess faith in Him without seeing Him

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Lam yakun is treated as a complete verb rather than an incomplete verb, like the usage in 4:17; the translation follows this grammatical reading.
rows.anchor: The translation of the verse has been done

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The omitted object of ‘denied’ is the Qur’an and the Messenger.
rows.anchor: The suppressed object is the Qur’ ān and the Messenger which they denied

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The People of the Book and idolaters are the two leading opposition groups; Qur’anic mushrikūn here is a proper noun for Quraysh or the Ishmaelites.
rows.anchor: were covert in this regard

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Min is partitive: the verse targets only the hostile subset, since both groups included Muslims, impartial people, and balanced non-Muslims whom the Qur’an praised.
rows.anchor: referred to here who were not willing

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Bayyinah means a manifest sign, specifically an undeniable miracle demanded by stubborn opponents, a demand the Qur’an mentions elsewhere.
rows.anchor: By such a manifest sign they meant that such a miracle be shown to them which they would not be able to deny

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The People of the Book demanded a heavenly book and had earlier demanded that Moses show them God; the idolaters likewise wanted individual open pages, as cited in 4:153 and 74:52.
rows.anchor: The People of the Book ask you to bring down directly for them a book from the heavens

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: These opponents reject revelation to one person and demand a separate scripture for each of them before accepting that God revealed guidance.
rows.anchor: their demand is that for each of them a separate scripture be revealed

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The demanded sign is an angel sent directly by God, not a human messenger who claims revelation; the angel must recite pure pages.
rows.anchor: they wanted some angel directly sent by the Almighty who would read untouched and pure pages

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A ṣaḥīfah is a page; the opponents would not accept an angel merely reporting God’s messages but wanted them written and read aloud.
rows.anchor: whatever he brings in the name of God should be in fact written and read

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The pages’ purity means untouched by any human or jinn, with only God and angels having touched them.
rows.anchor: Except for God and the angels no one among men and jinn should have touched them

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The pages must contain clear, unambiguous directives rather than assorted stories.
rows.anchor: the written pages should not contain tales and stories from here and there
